text: In a village called Himlaya, among Lebanon's hills, a little girl named Boutroussieh learned to pray with her parents. She was born in 1832, and her mother was named Rafqa. When Boutroussieh was seven, her mother died. It was a great loss, and it did not disappear quickly. Her father faced money troubles, so for several years she lived away from home and worked in another household. She kept growing, learning, and looking for the path her life might take.

text: When she came home, people around her hoped she would marry. Boutroussieh felt called to give her life to God as a nun instead. This was her own choice, not an easy answer someone else picked for her. She went to the convent of Our Lady of Deliverance in Bikfaya. She remembered a strong feeling of joy as she prayed before Mary's icon, and understood it as a sign of her calling. No one else had to hear or feel exactly what she did for her choice to matter. She joined the sisters and promised to live a life of prayer and service.

text: Her days included real work. In Ghazir she helped in a seminary kitchen. In the time left over, she learned Arabic, handwriting, and mathematics, and helped younger girls study. Imagine the steady rhythm of a kitchen: preparing food, washing dishes, and finding a little time to practice letters. That is a picture of the kind of work she did, not a record of one particular morning. A person who teaches and cooks can love God through both kinds of work.

text: She was sent to teach children in Deir el-Kamar during years of frightening violence in Lebanon. A Church biography tells of one time when she protected a child by hiding the child beneath her robe. We do not know what that child said or did afterward. We do know that fear did not stop her from acting to protect someone small. Later, with another sister, she helped start a school for girls in Maad. Girls who had been left out of learning now had a place to begin. Her courage did not only show in danger; it showed in ordinary days of teaching.

text: When her first community changed, Boutroussieh had to decide where to go next. She prayed, asked for guidance, and later described a dream that helped her choose the Lebanese Maronite Order. A dream is part of her reported faith experience; it was not an event everybody could see. In 1871 she entered the monastery of Saint Simon in Aito. She received a new name, Sister Rafqa, after the mother she had lost. Her days there were quiet, shaped by prayer, shared duties, and life with other sisters.

text: Years later, her eyes began to hurt badly. Rafqa prayed in a way that connected her pain with Jesus' suffering, according to the Church's account of her life. But a child should never try to become sick or believe pain is what God wants from them. Her superior insisted that she get medical treatment. Treatment did not end the illness. Over time Rafqa lost her sight, and moving her body also grew difficult. The sisters still cared for her. She still belonged to their community; illness did not take away her worth.

text: In 1897 six sisters moved to a new monastery of Saint Joseph in Jrabta, and Rafqa went with them. The sisters planted, prayed, and worked together. As her illness progressed, there were many things she could no longer do. Yet her hands could still knit socks and make clothing. Picture the feel of yarn passing carefully between her fingers. We cannot know what she thought in any one moment, but we can see that this was one way she kept taking part in the life around her. Receiving care and offering a small gift can both belong in the same life.

text: Rafqa died in 1914, after a long life that held childhood loss, work, teaching, prayer, and years of illness. The Church later studied her life, and Pope John Paul II proclaimed her a saint in 2001. People still visit the monastery at Jrabta to pray. Her story is not a promise that prayer will make illness go away. It is a story about a person whose dignity did not shrink when her body grew weaker, and about the sisters who stayed beside her.

text: What can you carry from Rafqa's life? You might remember the child she protected, the girls she taught, or the socks she made when her world had become very small. No one has to do every kind thing. You can notice one person, listen, and offer the help that is actually useful. When someone is sick, ask a trusted adult how to help and let trained caregivers do their work. When you are hurting, tell someone safe. Asking for help is also a brave way to care for the life God gave you.

title: Points of reflection
points: First, Rafqa protected a child in a dangerous time. Jesus taught his followers to care for those who are vulnerable. If someone near you seems unsafe, which trusted adult can you tell?
Second, she taught girls who needed a place to learn. God's call to love our neighbors can look like patient, everyday work. What could you help someone learn without making them feel small?

Third, the sisters cared for Rafqa when she could no longer see, and she still found ways to contribute. Every person has dignity, whether they need help or can give it. How can you listen to someone before deciding what help they need?

Fourth, she prayed through hard years, but she also received care. You do not have to be hurt to be close to God. If you are hurting, what prayer and what conversation with a trusted person could help you today?
